claims.text: On 07/01/26, the patient presented with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden onset after exertion, throbbing, diffuse, and associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, or focal neurological deficits.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, does not smoke, consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week, and engages in regular jogging.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines in the immediate family, though the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.

Initial observations on 07/01/26 recorded a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.

Initial neurological examinations on 07/01/26 were unremarkable, showing the patient alert and oriented with no focal deficits, normal cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed at 14:45 on 07/01/26 showed no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected at 15:15 on 07/01/26 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP of 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 07/01/26, the diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) was suspected based on clinical presentation and CT findings, and the patient was admitted to the Neurology ward.
On 07/01/26, oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours was initiated to manage vasospasm.
On 07/01/26, the patient's headache persisted at 7/10 intensity, blood pressure was 150/92 mmHg, and blood tests showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
On 07/01/26, oral potassium chloride (KCl) 1 g twice daily was prescribed to correct hypokalemia.
On 07/01/26 at 20:00, the patient's GP was contacted to provide an update on the admission and preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.
On 08/01/26, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS, the headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, CRP was 12 mg/L, and mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) persisted.
On 08/01/26, the nimodipine dose was adjusted to 30 mg orally every 4 hours, and a repeat MRA was planned for 48 hours later to assess resolution.
On 08/01/26, the patient received education on RCVS, including the importance of avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines.
On 09/01/26, the headache severity further reduced to 3/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and blood tests from 08/01/26 showed mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L).
On 09/01/26, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures, restricting excessive fluid intake, and repeating the MRA in 24 hours.
On 09/01/26, the rehab team assessed the patient, noting mild residual neck stiffness but no significant functional impairments, and arranged for outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.
On 10/01/26, the headache intensity was 2/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and the patient remained on nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours with dietary measures for hyponatremia.
On 10/01/26, a repeat MRA was planned for 11/01/26, and the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management and lifestyle modifications.
On 11/01/26, the headache was rated 2/10, blood pressure was 125/78 mmHg, and the patient was continuing nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours pending repeat MRA results.
On 11/01/26 at 10:30, a repeat MRA showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS, and discharge was planned for 12/01/26.
On 11/01/26, outpatient neurology follow-up was arranged for 4 weeks post-discharge.
On 12/01/26, the patient reported no further headaches, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and the repeat MRA confirmed resolution of vasoconstriction.
On 12/01/26, discharge was planned with a regimen of nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, and a referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks.
On 12/01/26 at 12:00, the patient's GP was contacted, and a discharge medication of amlodipine 5 mg once daily was discussed for post-discharge management.

Medication records conflict regarding the discharge regimen: note-17 on 12/01/26 plans for nimodipine 30 mg four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, while note-18 on 12/01/26 states amlodipine 5 mg once daily was discussed with the GP for discharge.
